label: Yirmeyahu (Jeremiah) — Part 4 — Chapters 24–31
summary_plain: YHWH shows Yirmeyahu two baskets of figs — good figs and bad figs. The good figs are those sent into exile whom YHWH will watch over and bring back. YHWH says: You will seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart. I will be found by you and restore your fortunes and gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you. Rachel weeps for her children and refuses to be comforted — but YHWH says there is hope for your future. Behold, the days are coming when I will make a new covenant with the house of Yisra'EL and the house of Yehudah — not like the covenant I made with their fathers. I will put my Torah within them, and I will write it on their hearts.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the DSS Jeremiah manuscripts (4QJer-a through 4QJer-e) and the Orit Ge'ez. Yirmeyahu 31:31-34 is the defining covenant passage in the entire prophetic literature — the new covenant (berit hadashah). The DSS preserve this concept in the Damascus Document (CD), which describes the Qumran community as 'those who entered the new covenant in the land of Damascus.' The new covenant is not a replacement of the Torah — it is the Torah written on hearts instead of tablets. The mechanism changes (internal instead of external), but the content remains the Torah. No institutional mediation is required — 'they shall all know me, from the least to the greatest.'

key_terms.definition: YHWH shows Yirmeyahu two baskets of figs: good figs (the exiles carried to Babylon — YHWH will watch over them and restore them) and bad figs (those left in Yehudah and those who fled to Mitzrayim — they will be destroyed).
Yirmeyahu's letter to the Babylonian exiles: 'Seek the peace of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to YHWH on its behalf, for in its peace you will have peace.'
Yirmeyahu 29:7 — the exiles are to settle, plant gardens, multiply, and seek the shalom of their place of exile; the vision for exile is active presence and flourishing, not isolation.
Yirmeyahu 30-31 is the Book of Consolation: promises of restoration after the disaster, addressing both Yisra'el and Yehudah; it ends with the New Covenant declaration.

Yirmeyahu 31:31-34 — YHWH will make a new (khadasha) covenant with the house of Yisra'el and Yehudah; not like the Sinai covenant which they broke; he will write his Torah on their hearts; they shall all know him.

The New Covenant promise in Yirmeyahu 31:33: 'I will put my Torah within them, and I will write it on their hearts.' The covenant law becomes internalized — no need for external mediation because all will know YHWH directly.

Yirmeyahu 31:15 — 'Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted because they are no more.' Rachel, the ancestral mother of Efrayim (northern tribes), weeps for the exiled northern kingdom; YHWH promises: Refrain from weeping, they will return.

Yirmeyahu wears a wooden yoke symbolizing submission to Babylon; he confronts the false prophet Khananiyah who breaks the wooden yoke; YHWH replaces it with an iron yoke — the exile will not be short.
YHWH's repeated promise in the Book of Consolation: the exiles will return from every land where they were driven; Yerushalayim will be rebuilt; the covenant community will be restored on their land.

key_terms.term: 'I Know the Plans I Have for You'
key_terms.definition: Yirmeyahu 29:11 — 'For I know the plans I have for you, declares YHWH, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.' Given in the context of YHWH telling the exiles the exile will last 70 years.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of the two baskets of figs in Yirmeyahu 24?
faq.answer: The vision overturns the natural assumption: those exiled to Babylon (the apparently punished) are the good figs YHWH watches over for restoration; those left in Yehudah and those who fled to Mitzrayim (the apparently preserved) are the bad figs headed for destruction. YHWH's favor is not tied to physical location or apparent safety.

faq.question: What does the Letter to the Exiles teach about faithful life in a foreign land?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 29 is the most direct prophetic instruction on diaspora life in the Hebrew corpus. YHWH commands: settle down, build, plant, multiply, and seek the shalom of the city where you are sent. This is active, engaged presence — not isolation or waiting for rescue. The 70-year timeline is realistic: build lives, not temporary camps.

faq.question: What is the New Covenant in Yirmeyahu 31:31-34?
faq.answer: The New Covenant differs from Sinai in its mode: Torah written on hearts, not stone. The relationship is internalized — 'I will be their Creator, they shall be my people' — without requiring external teaching because all will know YHWH directly, 'from the least to the greatest.' YHWH will forgive iniquity and remember sin no more. This is the most explicit New Covenant text in the pre-Rabbinic corpus.

faq.question: Why is 'Rachel weeping for her children' significant in Yirmeyahu 31?
faq.answer: Rachel was the ancestral mother of Efrayim and Menashsheh — the northern tribes. By placing her weeping at Ramah (a staging point for deportees), Yirmeyahu gives voice to the grief of the entire northern exile. But the text does not end with grief: YHWH commands 'Restrain your voice from weeping... they shall come back from the land of the enemy' (31:16-17). The lament is real; so is the promise.

faq.question: What does the Yoke of Babylon sign in chapters 27-28 mean?
faq.answer: YHWH commands Yirmeyahu to wear a wooden yoke as a sign that all nations must submit to Nebuchadnezzar — YHWH's instrument. When Khananiyah the false prophet breaks the wooden yoke claiming YHWH will break Babylon's power within two years, Yirmeyahu responds: you have made it iron. YHWH then tells Yirmeyahu: Khananiyah will die that year because he has spoken rebellion. He died two months later.

faq.question: What is the 70-year exile in context?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 29:10 sets the exile at seventy years before YHWH restores the people. This is not a prediction about an individual's lifetime but a generational span: those deported will largely die in Babylon; their children and grandchildren will return. The 70-year figure frames the exile as real but bounded, and grounds the community's hope in something specific rather than vague.

faq.question: What does 'I know the plans I have for you' mean in its original context?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 29:11 — 'For I know the plans I have for you, plans for welfare (shalom) and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope' — is not a general prosperity promise. It is YHWH's specific word to the Babylonian exiles being told they will be there for 70 years. The welfare and future are real, but they come after a long, difficult exile — not as an immediate escape from hardship.

faq.question: How permanent is the New Covenant according to Yirmeyahu 31:35-37?
faq.answer: YHWH says the New Covenant is as permanent as the fixed order of the cosmos: 'If the sun, moon, and stars cease their fixed order, then the offspring of Yisra'el will cease to be a nation before me.' YHWH anchors the covenant's reliability to creation itself. No human failure can break this covenant the way Sinai was broken — YHWH himself writes Torah on the heart.

faq.question: What does the Book of Consolation say about YHWH healing the incurable wound?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 30:12-17 addresses the people as having an incurable wound, an injury that no one can heal. The nations say their wound is punishment from YHWH for their sins. YHWH agrees that it is punishment — but then declares: I will restore your health and heal your wounds. The one who inflicts is also the one who heals.

faq.question: Why does YHWH call Efrayim his firstborn in Yirmeyahu 31:9?
faq.answer: In the restoration poem of Yirmeyahu 31:7-9, YHWH gathers the remnant of Yisra'el including 'the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor' — the vulnerable who cannot travel quickly. YHWH leads them back with weeping and consolations, by rivers of water on a straight path. Calling Efrayim (the northern kingdom) his firstborn re-establishes the full covenant family, not just Yehudah.

faq.question: What does Yirmeyahu 31:34 mean when it says 'no longer shall each one teach his neighbor'?
faq.answer: The New Covenant will make external instruction about knowing YHWH unnecessary because every member of the covenant community will know him directly — internalized Torah. This is not abolishing teaching but describing the transformed condition: YHWH's direct relationship with each person makes him known from within rather than transmitted only through external teachers. It describes a community where covenant knowledge is as natural as breathing.
